title: India Is Buying Oil from Venezuela, Brazil, Angola and Nigeria. The Hormuz Shift May Be Permanent.
excerpt: With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed, Indian refiners have quietly restructured the country's entire crude oil supply chain. Venezuela is now India's fourth-largest supplier.
body:
Before February 28, India's oil map was simple. The country imported 90% of its crude, and the largest share flowed through a 33-kilometre strait between Iran and Oman. The Strait of Hormuz carried more than 40% of India's oil imports and nearly all of its liquefied petroleum gas.

The Iran war closed that route. Four months later, India's refiners have not just adapted — they have redrawn the map entirely.

## The New Supply Chain

According to preliminary data from Kpler, India raised crude oil imports from Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria in April and May to cover shortfalls caused by the conflict. The numbers signal more than a temporary fix.

Venezuela — a country India had all but stopped buying from during the tightest phase of U.S. sanctions — is on track to become India's fourth-largest oil supplier in May, with 12 million barrels loaded in April alone. That is the highest level of Indian imports of Venezuelan crude since February 2020.

Brazil and Angola have also seen significantly higher shipments to Indian ports, while Nigeria has re-emerged as a meaningful supplier after years of declining volumes. India continues to receive roughly 1.9 million barrels per day of Russian oil and approximately 41,000 barrels per day from Iraq, which routes around Hormuz through Turkey's Ceyhan pipeline.

For NRIs, this shift in sourcing may have financial implications, particularly for those involved in remittances or investments tied to oil prices. As India diversifies its oil imports, fluctuations in global oil prices can directly affect the value of remittances sent back home, impacting family budgets and investment strategies.

## A Structural Adjustment, Not a Stopgap

Oil Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said in recent remarks that India had expanded its crude procurement sources from 27 countries to 40, with Argentina the latest addition. Prime Minister Modi's visits to Nigeria, Brazil, and Guyana last November — the first by an Indian prime minister to Nigeria in 17 years — now appear prescient rather than ceremonial.

"This is less a temporary fix than a structural adjustment in sourcing strategy," Indian government officials told The Indian Eye. The diversification is driven partly by necessity and partly by economics: West African crude grades are currently cheaper than Middle Eastern benchmarks, and Latin American heavy crudes are well-suited to India's complex refinery configurations.

India's private-sector refiners — Reliance Industries and Nayara Energy in particular — have decades of experience processing heavy, sour crudes from Venezuela and elsewhere. Their ability to absorb these non-traditional grades gives India a degree of flexibility that many Asian importers lack.

For NRIs working in sectors reliant on stable oil prices, such as logistics or manufacturing, these changes could lead to shifts in job security and economic opportunities abroad. 

## The Costs of Rerouting

The shift is not painless. A voyage from Brazil's Santos terminal to Jamnagar, India takes 40 to 45 days — compared to 7 to 10 days from the Persian Gulf. Freight costs are $1.50 to $2.50 per barrel higher, and the extended transit times create additional working capital pressure.

There are also geopolitical risks in the new supply chain. Venezuelan crude flows depend on the whims of U.S. sanctions policy. Nigerian output remains vulnerable to pipeline sabotage in the Niger Delta. Brazilian exports compete with rising domestic demand from Petrobras.

And the fundamental problem remains unsolved. The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of the world's oil before the war. No combination of alternative suppliers can fully replace that volume. The International Energy Agency estimates the conflict has already cut global oil demand by 4 to 5 million barrels per day in April — a 4 to 5% reduction driven mostly by price-induced demand destruction.

## What It Means for India's Wallet

Brent crude traded near $95 a barrel on Monday, up more than 60% since the war began. Even with cheaper African and Latin American grades partially offsetting the Hormuz premium, India's total import bill has ballooned.

The RBI last week unveiled a $50 billion package to stabilise the rupee and attract dollar inflows, including concessional swap facilities for NRI deposits and state-run enterprise borrowings. The rupee, which hit record lows earlier this year, has recovered modestly but remains under pressure.

Economists at Aberdeen Investments warn that India faces "a series of supply shocks" beyond oil — including disruptions to fertiliser imports that could damage wheat production, particularly as farmers brace for El Niño conditions.

For NRIs, these economic pressures may translate into increased costs of living and challenges in sending money back home. India's oil basket may now be more diversified than it has ever been. Whether that diversity is enough to absorb a prolonged closure of the world's most important energy chokepoint remains the trillion-dollar question.
